Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

# Bookings API

The Bookings API lets your application create, move, and cancel appointments on a shared calendar without touching the underlying calendar provider directly. It handles the parts that are tedious to get right: overlapping holds, time zones that shift under daylight saving, and two clients trying to claim the same 10:00 slot within a few milliseconds of each other.

Everything is organised around three resources. A *calendar* is the bookable thing, whether that is a person, a meeting room, or a piece of equipment. An *availability rule* describes when that calendar can be booked, in recurring weekly blocks plus one-off exceptions. A *booking* is a confirmed claim on a span of time, and it always belongs to exactly one calendar. Those three cover every endpoint in the reference.

Requests and responses are JSON, timestamps are RFC 3339 with an explicit offset, and every write endpoint accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header so that a retried request after a network timeout does not produce a duplicate booking. Read the conventions page once and you can skip the boilerplate in every later section.

This guide starts with authentication and a first booking you can make in about five minutes. From there it covers availability queries, recurrence, webhooks for cancellations made outside your app, and the error codes you will hit in production.

If you are migrating from v1, start with the migration notes instead. The slot model changed, and the old `/slots/reserve` call has no direct equivalent.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on authentication.

Authentication uses a bearer token sent in the `Authorization` header. Tokens are scoped per calendar set, so a token issued for the sales team's calendars returns 403 on a booking that belongs to support. Create tokens in the dashboard under Settings, API keys; each one carries an explicit scope list such as `bookings:write` or `availability:read`, and a token missing the scope an endpoint needs fails with `error.code` set to `insufficient_scope` rather than a generic 401. Server-side calls should use a secret key. For browser or mobile clients, mint a short-lived client token from your backend instead, since it expires in 15 minutes and cannot list calendars it was not granted. Rotating a key does not invalidate the old one immediately: both stay valid for 24 hours so you can redeploy without dropped requests.

Rewrite it for someone who has never used a REST API before.

# Bookings API

An API is a way for one program to ask another program to do something. This one manages appointments. Your software sends a message over the internet saying "book Tuesday at 10:00," and the Bookings API writes that into a calendar and sends back a confirmation. You never have to connect to Google Calendar or Outlook yourself.

The API takes care of the fiddly problems that appointment software runs into. When two people click "book" on the same slot at the same moment, only one of them gets it. When someone in Tokyo books with someone in Chicago, both see the right local time. Clocks jump forward for daylight saving and the appointment stays where it belongs. None of that logic has to live in your code.

There are three things to learn, and they are the whole system. A *calendar* is whatever can be booked, such as a hairdresser, a conference room, or a tennis court. An *availability rule* says when it is open, like "Monday to Friday, 9 to 5, closed December 25." A *booking* is one appointment on one calendar, and it sits inside the hours the rule allows. Everything else in this guide is built out of those three, so it is worth reading this paragraph twice before you go on. If a later chapter confuses you, come back here first.

Messages travel in a format called JSON: text that both humans and programs can read. Times are written with the time zone attached, so `2026-03-14T10:00:00-05:00` means 10 in the morning, five hours behind UTC.

The first chapter walks you through making a single booking, start to finish. Follow it typing everything out, even the parts you do not understand yet. Later chapters go back over each piece and explain what it was doing and why it was there.

Add a short warning about rate limits.

output: Rate limits apply per token: 60 requests a minute, and 10 bookings a minute on any single calendar. Go over either and the API returns status 429 with a `Retry-After` header telling you how many seconds to wait. This bites hardest when you import an existing schedule, since a loop that creates 500 bookings as fast as it can will be throttled partway through. Add a pause between calls, or send them in batches of 10 with a one second gap.
